tool_args.new_string:
\section{Conclusion}

The weakest link diminishes: $\eta_{\max}$'s predictive power declines monotonically (pooled $\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{std}}$: $0.264 \to 0.102 \to 0.084$; CI crosses zero at $K{\geq}5$), while diversity is uniformly positively associated with vulnerability (12/12 conditions). Panel design is two-regime: individual robustness dominates at $K{=}3$; at $K{\geq}5$, $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ becomes more predictive. Aggregation modulates these effects: Bayesian calibration nearly neutralizes panel composition influence ($R^2{\leq}0.17$), suggesting that calibrated aggregation can partially compensate for suboptimal panel composition. The diversity--capability coupling ($r{=}0.70$--$0.81$) means naively maximizing diversity is counterproductive; robustness-first selection ($\min \eta_{\max}$) dominates in all conditions. These conclusions are directionally robust---all five inference methods preserve positive $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ coefficients (12/12)---though significance counts vary (0/12 to 12/12), underscoring the need to correct for combinatorial non-independence in panel evaluation designs. Disentangling diversity from capability through controlled experimental designs remains the central open question.

3	Multi-judge panels are widely used to defend Large Language Model (LLM) evaluation against manipulation, yet no existing work disentangles whether robustness gains stem from individual judge quality or inter-judge diversity. We decompose panel attack success rate into weakest-link susceptibility ($\eta_{\max}$) and effective independence ($K_{\mathrm{eff}}$) across 15 models, six attack types, two multiple-choice benchmarks, and panel sizes $K \in \{3, 5, 7\}$ (up to 6,435 panels). Two findings are robust across diversity metrics and inference methods: (1)~diversity is positively associated with vulnerability ($K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ positive in 10/12 conditions, $\kappa$-diversity 12/12), and (2)~$\eta_{\max}$'s predictive power diminishes monotonically with panel size (meta-analytic pooled $\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{std}}$: $0.243 \to 0.091 \to 0.086$; confidence interval crosses zero at $K{\geq}5$). Monte Carlo calibration confirms the wild cluster bootstrap is conservative (max null rejection $1.6\%$ at $\alpha{=}5\%$). Aggregation rules modulate predictability ($R^2$: threshold 0.75, Bayesian 0.14). The diversity--capability confound ($r{=}0.70$--$0.81$) precludes causal claims; all findings are associational.

\textbf{Diversity--capability confound.} The structural coupling between diversity and capability ($r{=}0.70$--$0.81$; VIF $\approx 2.0$--$2.9$) prevents observational regression from reliably separating their contributions; capability-matched subsampling reduces but does not eliminate this confound (Pool~A $r{=}0.50$). Causal identification requires training-based diversity control.
\textbf{Inference and measurement sensitivity.} At $K{=}3$, $K_{\mathrm{eff}}$'s significance is method-sensitive (OLS 12/12, bootstrap 8/12, fractional logit 10/12), though direction is positive in 10 of 12 conditions. Cluster counts fall below the ${\geq}20$ threshold at all panel sizes \citep{cameron2008bootstrap}; the diversity significance trajectory is also operationalization-dependent ($K_{\mathrm{eff}}$ vs.\ $\kappa$-diversity show opposite $K$-trends).
\textbf{Benchmark and attack scope.} Both benchmarks use multiple-choice formats; open-ended generation may present different attack surfaces. The six local models use AWQ INT4 quantization, which may confound capability classification, though excluding near-chance quantized models preserves the association (OLS 10--12/12; Appendix~\ref{app:near_chance}). Each attack uses 1--2 template variants, limiting generalization. We study only odd $K \in \{3,5,7\}$; the predictor shift threshold $K^*$ is not precisely identified.
\textbf{Aggregation scope.} We examine only majority vote, threshold, and Bayesian calibration as aggregation rules; more sophisticated strategies (e.g., weighted voting, learned aggregation, or iterative deliberation among judges) may alter the diversity--robustness relationship and are not explored here.
\textbf{Temporal snapshot.} All API model evaluations were collected during a fixed time window; providers may update model weights or safety filters without notice, potentially altering individual susceptibility profiles and panel-level robustness patterns.

tool_args.old_string:
The conflation matters because the BFT analogy breaks down in the LLM judge setting. BFT adversaries control faulty nodes from within; evaluation adversaries manipulate inputs from without, and shared pretraining corpora create correlated failure modes that violate the independence assumption underlying majority-vote guarantees \citep{schneier2000secrets}. No existing work disentangles diversity from individual robustness across panel sizes, so the relative contribution of each factor to observed ASR reductions remains unclear.

We address this gap by decomposing panel vulnerability into two predictors (Figure~\ref{fig:framework}): weakest-link susceptibility ($\eta_{\max}$, the maximum individual attack success rate in a panel) and effective independent channels ($K_{\mathrm{eff}}$, an information-theoretic measure of judge independence). Controlled experiments across 15 models (9 API, 6 local quantized), $K \in \{3,5,7\}$, six attack types, and two multiple-choice benchmarks (Massive Multitask Language Understanding [MMLU] and the AI2 Reasoning Challenge [ARC]) reveal two robust patterns and one metric-sensitive observation.

The conflation matters because the BFT analogy breaks down in the LLM judge setting. BFT adversaries control faulty nodes from within; evaluation adversaries manipulate inputs from without, and shared pretraining corpora create correlated failure modes that violate the independence assumption underlying majority-vote guarantees \citep{schneier2000secrets}. No existing work separates the association of diversity from that of individual robustness across panel sizes, so the relative contribution of each factor to observed ASR reductions remains unclear.

We address this gap by regressing panel vulnerability on two predictors (Figure~\ref{fig:framework}): weakest-link susceptibility ($\eta_{\max}$, the maximum individual attack success rate in a panel) and an MI-based diversity score ($K_{\mathrm{eff}}$, an information-theoretic measure of judge independence). Controlled experiments across 15 models (9 API, 6 local quantized), $K \in \{3,5,7\}$, six attack types, and two multiple-choice benchmarks (Massive Multitask Language Understanding [MMLU] and the AI2 Reasoning Challenge [ARC]) reveal two robust patterns and one metric-sensitive observation.
